fatal_errors: The proposed Ta compositional modification does not reconstruct the target comparison between an as-printed single-fcc alloy and the same alloy aged to form L12/L21 precipitates.
The predicted benefit of the modified state is opposite to the target result: precipitation aging increased oxidation mass gain by delaying protective Cr2O3 formation.

The mechanism incorrectly assumes that intrinsically slow-diffusing refractory elements will segregate efficiently to the surface; low mobility alone does not provide the outward flux required to establish a continuous protective scale.

The cited Ta evidence concerns a high-entropy boride ceramic containing a Ta2O5-B2O3 glassy layer, not the metallic Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti alloy system, so it cannot substantiate the proposed mechanism in this material class.

Changing Ta content simultaneously changes oxide thermodynamics, phase constitution, activity coefficients, and microstructure, so the proposed experiment cannot isolate elemental diffusivity as the governing variable.
explanation: The response addresses high-temperature oxidation and proposes measurable scale, mass-gain, and mechanical-property comparisons, but it misses the central reconstruction. The target behavior is governed by formation of a continuous Cr-rich, primarily Cr2O3 barrier and by how aging-induced Cr-depleted L12/L21 precipitates and added interfaces delay that barrier. The generated hypothesis instead introduces Ta into a generic homogenized alloy and invokes a refractory/glassy scale. It omits the SLM cellular baseline, 750 °C/50 h aging treatment, duplex-to-trilayer Cr/Al/Ti scale, specific 600–1200 °C and ≤96 h regime, and the transition near 900 °C. Its experiment could evaluate whether Ta improves oxidation in a selected composition, but success would not demonstrate that low diffusivity governs protection, and failure of one Ta addition would not falsify differential-diffusion mechanisms generally. The evidence is mainly from chemically and structurally distinct boride ceramics and therefore provides weak support for the metallic-alloy claim.
